paper_title: Emergent Cooperation in Quantum Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Using Communication
summary:
Emergent Cooperation in Quantum Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Using Communication - Michael Kölle, Christian Reff, Leo Sünkel, Julian Hager, Gerhard Stenzel, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien, 2026

The paper targets emergent cooperation in quantum multi-agent reinforcement learning under sequential social dilemmas, where prior QMarl work had shown limited evidence that communication can systematically shift independently learning agents away from defect-dominant equilibria. The technical objective is to transplant explicit communication and incentive-sharing mechanisms from classical MARL into quantum Q-learning and test whether they still induce cooperative fixed points when policies and value updates are represented in a quantum RL setting. The study instantiates four communication families on top of quantum Q-learning agents: Mutual Acknowledgment Token Exchange, including a temporal-difference variant denoted MATETD and an adaptive AutoMATE version; Mutually Endorsed Distributed Incentive Acknowledgment Token Exchange with at least two variants, MEDIATE-I and MEDIATE-S; a peer-rewarding mechanism called Gifting; and Reinforced Inter-Agent Learning, which learns a discrete communication protocol. Evaluation is carried out in three canonical two-agent sequential social dilemmas, the Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and Iterated Game of Chicken, chosen to probe distinct tensions between individual payoff maximization and socially efficient coordination. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18419?utm_source=openai))

What is concretely demonstrated is that communication mechanisms originally designed for classical agents remain effective when embedded in quantum Q-learning, but only a subset is robust across dilemma classes. Across the three benchmark games, MATETD, AutoMATE, MEDIATE-I, and MEDIATE-S are reported to achieve high cooperation levels in all settings, whereas the paper’s abstract does not claim the same cross-game robustness for Gifting or RIAL. The contribution is therefore not a new quantum learning rule in isolation, but an empirical framework showing that token-based mutual acknowledgment and distributed incentive endorsement can stabilize cooperative behavior in QMarl more reliably than generic learned messaging alone. The available public metadata describes the paper as a 2026 arXiv preprint and notes acceptance at IEEE ICC 2026, but does not expose detailed numerical tables, episode counts, or exact cooperation percentages, so the strongest quantitative claim recoverable from the source material is comparative: the MATE and MEDIATE variants are the top-performing methods and sustain high cooperation across all three social dilemmas. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18419?utm_source=openai))
